passage:
Monday. Akash emailed the audit team about the false safety logs in the warehouse. By evening his manager said, "Thanks for flagging it. Let's keep this between us."

Thursday. Akash was dropped from the planning meeting. His name disappeared from the project chart, and a colleague whispered that people were calling him "the troublemaker." He felt hot with disbelief. He began saving every email and note in a folder at home.

The following Tuesday. Akash spoke with his friend Jahnavi, who works at a legal aid clinic, and she helped him work out which regulator to write to and how to describe the timeline. He also told two close friends how he felt. It hurt to be sidelined for doing right, but he kept sleeping, keeping records and turning up.

By the end of that week, he had sent his complaint to the regulator, and he still felt like himself.

qa.q: What did Akash email the audit team about?
qa.a: Akash emailed the audit team about false safety logs in the warehouse.

qa.q: How did Akash feel when he was dropped from the planning meeting?
qa.a: Akash felt hot with disbelief and hurt at being punished after doing the right thing.

qa.q: What steps did Akash take to protect himself after being sidelined?
qa.a: Akash saved every email and note, got help from Jahnavi at a legal aid clinic, talked to close friends and wrote to the regulator.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have seen Akash's situation?
qa.a: Jahnavi may have seen it as a familiar pattern of retaliation, which is why she helped him focus on records and the right regulator instead of blaming himself.

grounding: After reporting an issue, Akash is sidelined and labelled a troublemaker; he keeps records, gets advice, leans on friends and keeps his integrity.

passage:
Three months after Disha reported the falsified lab-test certificates at the Pune construction firm, her name disappeared from the weekly project emails. Yogesh, her manager, started calling her "our little activist" in meetings. Her desk was moved next to the printer.
Some nights she sat on the balcony and wondered if she'd ruined her life for a few pieces of paper.
Then she opened a folder on her laptop called "Record". Every excluded email, every comment, dated. Her friend Ritu, a lawyer, said the retaliation was real, and gave her the number of the labour commissioner's office. On Sunday, her college friends came over with pav bhaji and let her talk for three hours.
On Monday Disha walked into the office, head up, and set her tea next to the printer. It had a cost. But she could still look at herself in the mirror.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling on the balcony at night?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and alone, wondering if she had ruined her life by reporting the certificates.

qa.q: What steps helped Disha cope with the retaliation?
qa.a: She kept dated records, got advice from a lawyer friend about the labour commissioner's office, and leaned on her friends.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see Disha's report?
qa.a: Yogesh seems to see her as a threat or a troublemaker, and his mocking "activist" label shows resentment rather than respect.

grounding: After reporting an issue the protagonist is sidelined and labelled a troublemaker; she keeps records, seeks legal advice, leans on friends, and keeps her integrity.

passage:
"They took me off the Chennai audit, Irfan. Just like that. After I reported the fake invoices."
"Who told you?"
"Nobody. I found out from the schedule. And today in the corridor, someone said, 'Careful, Afreen's listening,' and laughed."
"Afreen, this is retaliation. It's not in your head, and it's not your fault."
"It feels like my fault. Like I should have kept quiet."
"You reported fraud. Do you have copies of what you submitted?"
"Yes. And the email where they acknowledged it."
"Keep every change, every comment. Dates. I'll send you the name of an employment lawyer my sister used."
"What if nothing changes?"
"Then at least you'll know you did the right thing, and you'll have proof." Irfan passed her a plate of biryani. "Also, eat. You're coming to my place every Friday until this is over."
Afreen laughed, her eyes wet. "Every Friday?"
"Every Friday."

qa.q: How did Afreen find out she was taken off the Chennai audit?
qa.a: From the schedule; nobody told her.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she said "It feels like my fault"?
qa.a: She felt guilty and doubtful, as though she should have kept quiet, even though she had reported fraud.

qa.q: What did Irfan advise Afreen to do?
qa.a: Keep dated records of every change and comment, keep the acknowledgment email, and contact an employment lawyer.

qa.q: How might Irfan see Afreen's situation?
qa.a: Irfan sees clear retaliation and wants her to know it's not her fault, and offers steady support every Friday.

grounding: After reporting fraud the protagonist is sidelined and mocked; a friend helps her see it is retaliation, keep records, seek a lawyer and lean on friends.
